groups.high: A content licence permits Facebook to use material without transferring the user's intellectual-property ownership. The Facebook terms describe a non-exclusive, transferable, sub-licensable, royalty-free, worldwide licence for protected content uploaded or shared in connection with its products, consistent with privacy and application settings. Non-exclusive means the owner can use the material and permit others to use it. Transferable and sub-licensable describe permissions Meta can pass or grant onward; they do not mean the user is assigning copyright. Royalty-free means this contractual permission does not require a royalty payment. Worldwide describes its geographic scope. The licence supports activities such as hosting, copying, distributing, displaying, translating, modifying, and creating derivative works. It should not be expanded into an unlimited right over all personal data: copyright permission, privacy rights, and lawful processing obligations are distinct. Nor should it be described as necessarily perpetual and irrevocable. The terms link the licence's end to deletion from Meta's systems, with qualifications for the deletion process, certain retention obligations, and material other people have shared or used under the licence. Account deletion is therefore not proof that every copy disappears immediately. Privacy settings matter to permitted sharing but do not prevent every independent recipient from keeping a copy. Before posting, consider the audience, whether you have rights to the material, and whether you are comfortable granting the stated uses. The applicable version of Facebook's terms governs; do not infer a permanent, unconditional grant from the word worldwide alone.
groups.mid: Posting a photo on Facebook does not mean you give Meta your copyright. You still own the rights in content you created, but the Facebook terms give Meta a licence, which is permission to use protected content you upload or share. That permission is non-exclusive, transferable, sub-licensable, royalty-free, and worldwide. Here is what those terms mean. Non-exclusive lets you keep using your work and give others permission too, while transferable lets Meta pass its permission onward. Sub-licensable lets it give others permission under the licence. Neither means you have handed over ownership. Royalty-free means Meta does not owe a royalty for these permitted uses, while worldwide means the permission is not limited to one country. The listed uses include hosting, copying, distributing, showing, translating, changing, and making new works from your content. They must be consistent with your privacy and app settings. This is not an unlimited licence over every kind of personal data. Your copyright rights and your privacy rights are separate. Does the permission last forever? You should not assume that. The terms connect the end of the licence to deletion from Meta's systems, with exceptions and conditions. Deletion can take time. Some records may need to be kept, and content shared or used by other people may remain. Deleting your account therefore does not prove that every copy is gone. Your sharing settings matter, but another person may still keep a copy they received. Before posting, check who can see the content. Check that you have the rights to share it. Read the version of Facebook's terms that applies to you. A worldwide licence is broad, but that word alone does not make it permanent or unconditional.
groups.low: If you post your own photo on Facebook, you do not give up your copyright. You still own your work, but you give Meta a licence. That means you let it use the content you post or share. The terms call this permission non-exclusive, transferable, sub-licensable, royalty-free, and worldwide. Those are long words, so let us unpack them. Non-exclusive means you can still use your work and let other people use it. Transferable means Meta can pass its permission on. Sub-licensable means it can let someone else use the work under that permission. You have not given them ownership. Royalty-free means Meta does not have to pay a royalty for these uses. Worldwide means the permission can apply in any country. Meta can host, copy, share, show, translate, change, and make new works from the content. These uses must fit your privacy and app settings. This is a content licence, not a right to do anything with all your personal data. Privacy rights still matter too. Does the licence last forever? Do not assume that. The terms link its end to deletion from Meta's systems, but there are conditions. Deletion may take time. Some records may have to stay. Copies that others shared or used under the licence may remain too. So deleting an account does not prove that every copy has gone. Your settings help control sharing. They cannot make every person delete a copy they already got. Before you post, check who can see it and whether you have the right to share it. Check the terms that apply to your account. Worldwide does not mean forever or without limits.
groups.source_review: Official Facebook terms URL was login/rate-limit blocked. Licence wording corroborated in a reproduced terms text; version-specific deletion exceptions require further primary-page review. Not claimed as comprehensive current legal verification.
groups.notes: Removed original unsupported perpetual/irrevocable assertion, incorrect transfer direction, and unlimited personal-data/AI-use inference. Preserved ownership, licence features and valid practical distinctions.

groups.high: The U.S. TikTok privacy-policy clause referenced in this topic states that TikTok may collect biometric identifiers and biometric information, including faceprints and voiceprints, from user content. Where applicable law requires permission, the clause says the required permission will be sought before collection. This is a qualified collection statement, not proof that every uploaded video generates an identity template or that a particular identification algorithm is deployed. Biometric information concerns measurable human characteristics. A faceprint can represent facial features numerically; a voiceprint can represent characteristics of a speaker's voice. These differ from recognizing an object in a video or transcribing spoken words. The policy also describes analysis of image and audio content, including objects, scenery, facial or bodily features, audio characteristics, and spoken text. Such analysis does not invariably constitute identity recognition. The clause should not be treated as a technical specification of geometric measurements, cryptographic signatures, moderation systems, or cross-platform identification. Likewise, an unspecified retention period must not be converted into a precise storage guarantee. Permissions and privacy rights depend on the applicable U.S. law and policy version; the clause does not erase statutory protections. Before uploading identifiable faces or voices, consider whose information the content contains, review the relevant privacy and permission notices, and use the available privacy-request channels. A face or voice may remain recognizable even when a username changes. The important distinction is between what the policy permits, what the service actually does in a particular situation, and what the law requires.
groups.mid: TikTok's U.S. privacy-policy clause says it may collect biometric information from content users provide. The examples named are faceprints and voiceprints. Biometric information is data about measurable features of a person. A faceprint can turn facial features into a numerical pattern. A voiceprint can describe features of a person's voice. These patterns are different from spotting a chair in a video or writing down the words someone says. The policy also describes looking at images and audio for objects, scenery, face and body features, sounds, and spoken text. That kind of analysis does not always identify a person. Does this prove that TikTok makes an identity template from every video? No. The words may collect do not tell us which system was used for each upload. They also do not prove that the patterns are cryptographic signatures or that a named moderation algorithm uses them. The clause says TikTok will seek required permission before collection where the law requires it. Your rights depend on the applicable U.S. law and the policy version. The clause does not cancel those rights. Nor does an unclear storage period give us a precise promise about when each faceprint will be deleted. Before uploading a face or voice, think about whose information is in the clip. Read the privacy and permission notices, and check the available ways to make a privacy request. Changing a username does not change someone's face or voice. Keep three things separate: what the policy allows, what actually happens to a particular upload, and what the law requires.
groups.low: TikTok's U.S. privacy-policy clause says it may collect faceprints and voiceprints from your content. These are types of biometric data. That means data about features of a person. A faceprint can be a number pattern made from a face. A voiceprint can be a pattern made from a voice. This is not the same as finding a chair in a clip. It is not the same as turning speech into written words. The policy also describes checking images and sound. That may include objects, places, face and body features, sounds, and spoken words. Not all of those checks tell the app who a person is. Does may collect mean it makes a faceprint from every video? No. The clause does not tell us what happens to each upload. It does not prove that a faceprint is a secret code or that a named safety system uses it. Where the law requires permission, the clause says TikTok will seek it before collection. The law and the policy version matter to your rights. The clause does not take those rights away. It also does not give us an exact time for how long each faceprint is kept. Before you upload a face or voice, think about who is in the clip. Read the privacy and permission notices. Check how you can make a privacy request. A new username does not give you a new face or voice. Keep these questions apart: What does the policy allow? What happened to this upload? What does the law require?
groups.source_review: Official U.S. policy clause retrieved through indexed primary-source text; direct open failed. Answer is explicitly scoped to the referenced clause, not a claim that the same edition is current in every jurisdiction.
groups.notes: Removed invented algorithm, cryptographic-signature, exact-purpose and cross-platform identification claims. Preserved biometric concepts and qualified may/where-required-by-law wording.

groups.high: Cross-app and cross-site tracking allows activity outside Instagram to inform the information Meta associates with an account or device. Meta describes receiving information from advertisers, app developers, publishers, and other partners through business tools, including the Meta Pixel, APIs, SDKs, social plugins, and Facebook Login. A pixel is website code; an SDK is software incorporated into an app. Partners may report events such as visits, purchases, or use of a service together with identifiers that support matching. Meta may combine this with activity on its own services for advertising and personalization, subject to the applicable policy, consent requirements, and controls. It does not follow that every website, every app, every click, or every private message is visible to Meta. The presence of a measurement tool is not proof of unrestricted access to the entire device. Cookies, advertising identifiers, and other matching mechanisms have different roles and limitations. Device permissions, browser restrictions, and service settings can constrain some activity but should not be described as a universal off switch. Privacy controls for activity received from other businesses address particular uses or associations; the exact effect and available controls depend on the policy and region. Do not equate disconnecting an activity association with deleting every underlying record. The core concern is that a shopping or browsing event outside Instagram may contribute to the profile used on it. Review the partner site's notice, relevant device permissions, and Meta's current activity and advertising controls before assuming either that no information is shared or that all sharing is unavoidable.
groups.mid: Instagram can be affected by things you do outside the app. Meta says advertisers, app makers, publishers, and other partners can send it information. They use tools such as the Meta Pixel, APIs, SDKs, social plugins, and Facebook Login. A pixel is code on a website. An SDK is software built into an app. An API lets services exchange information. A shop could report a visit or purchase. It could send an identifier too. That is a code used to match the event to an account or device. Meta may combine partner information with activity on its own services for ads and personalization. The policy, legal consent rules, and available controls still apply. This does not mean Meta can see every website, app, click, or private message. A tracking tool does not give it unlimited access to your phone. Cookies and advertising identifiers can help with matching, but each has limits. Browser rules, device permissions, and service settings can limit some tracking. None should be assumed to stop every kind of data sharing. Meta also has controls for activity received from other businesses. What these controls do depends on the policy and where you live. You may be able to disconnect activity from an account. That does not mean every record is deleted. The main point is simple: a shopping or browsing event elsewhere may help shape the profile used on Instagram. Check the shop or app's privacy notice, your device permissions, and Meta's current activity and ad settings. Do not assume that nothing is shared, or that you have no choices at all.
groups.low: Something you do outside Instagram may affect what you see inside it. Meta says shops, app makers, publishers, and other partners can send it data. They can use the Meta Pixel, APIs, SDKs, social plugins, or Facebook Login. A pixel is code on a website. An SDK is software inside an app. An API lets services pass data to each other. A shop might send a visit or purchase with a code that helps match it to an account or device. Meta may join that data with what you do on its own services. This can help choose ads or other content. The privacy policy, consent rules, and available controls still matter. It does not mean Meta sees every app, click, website, or private message. A tool on a site does not let Meta see your whole phone. Cookies and ad IDs may help match data, but they have limits. Your browser, phone permissions, and app settings may block some uses. Do not assume one switch stops all sharing. Meta has controls for activity it gets from other businesses too. What they do can depend on where you live and the policy that applies. Disconnecting an activity from your account may not delete every record. So a visit or purchase elsewhere may help build the profile used on Instagram. Check that site's notice, your phone permissions, and Meta's current activity and ad settings. You should not assume that nothing is shared. But you should not assume you have no choices either.
groups.source_review: Primary Meta notices and explanations checked for partner tools, off-platform activity and control changes. Avoided implying a single timeless settings interface or universal tracking ability.
groups.notes: Removed surveillance rhetoric, universal fingerprinting/profile claims and unsupported statements that all apps/devices are seamlessly mapped. Preserved supported tool names and privacy distinctions.

groups.high: End-to-end encryption protects a message between its communicating endpoints; it does not prevent an intended business recipient from reading what the customer sends. WhatsApp's explanation of business conversations distinguishes the encrypted delivery path from the business's arrangements for managing received messages. Its 2020 explanation describes chats with businesses using WhatsApp Messenger, the WhatsApp Business app, or a self-hosted Business API as end-to-end encrypted. Where a business appoints a third-party vendor to operate the API and access messages on its behalf, that explanation does not classify the resulting arrangement as end-to-end encrypted, including when Facebook is that hosting vendor. This is an architectural and version-specific distinction, not a claim that all business chats lose transport protection. WhatsApp states that the Signal protocol protects delivery and that there is no encryption off switch. After delivery, authorized employees or providers may handle the business's copy, potentially including storage, support, or marketing uses subject to applicable law and the business's privacy practices. Facebook's role as a hosting processor was described as processing at the business's instruction, not automatic use of message contents to choose Meta advertisements. The business might nevertheless use received chats for its own marketing. Assess the recipient and any disclosed hosting provider as well as the encryption indication. Avoid sending unnecessary sensitive data, and ask about access, retention, and privacy notices. This topic concerns the referenced business-hosting explanation; current product architecture and disclosures should be checked separately rather than treating a historical API description as a universal current rule.
groups.mid: If you send a message to a business, that business can read it. Encryption does not hide it from the business you sent it to. End-to-end encryption protects the path between the chat's endpoints. WhatsApp's 2020 explanation described different business setups. Chats using WhatsApp Messenger, the WhatsApp Business app, or a self-hosted Business API were called end-to-end encrypted. Self-hosted means the business runs that system itself. But a business might hire a third-party vendor to run its API and read messages for it. WhatsApp did not call that whole setup end-to-end encrypted. This also applied if Facebook was the hosting vendor. That did not mean all business chats lacked encryption. The Signal protocol still protected delivery. The explanation said there was no switch to turn encryption off. What happens after a business gets the message? Its authorized staff or service providers may handle its copy. They may keep it or use it for customer support. Marketing use must still fit the law and the business's privacy practices. Facebook as host was described as acting on the business's instructions. That did not mean your message would automatically be used to choose Meta ads. But the business might use received chats for its own marketing. Check the recipient, any named host, and the encryption notice. Ask who can read your messages and how long they keep copies. Avoid sending extra private details that are not needed. This explains the older hosting notice. Check current product notices too, since business setups can change.
groups.low: If you send a message to a shop, the shop can read it. Encryption does not hide it from the person you meant to send it to. End-to-end encryption protects the path between the chat's endpoints. WhatsApp's 2020 explanation also described different business setups. Chats using WhatsApp Messenger, the WhatsApp Business app, or a self-hosted Business API were called end-to-end encrypted. Self-hosted means the business runs that system itself. But a business might hire a third-party vendor to run its API and read messages for it. WhatsApp did not call that whole setup end-to-end encrypted. This also applied if Facebook was the hosting vendor. That did not mean all business chats had no encryption. The Signal protocol still protected delivery. The explanation said there was no switch to turn encryption off. What happens after a shop gets the message? Its staff or allowed service providers may use the shop's copy. They may keep it or use it to help you. Any marketing use still has to fit the law and the shop's privacy practices. Facebook as host was described as acting on the business's instructions. That did not mean your message would automatically be used to pick Meta ads. But the shop might use chats for its own marketing. Look at the recipient, any named host, and the encryption notice. Ask who can read your messages and how long they keep them. Do not send extra private details that are not needed. This explains the older hosting notice. Check today's product notices too, since business setups can change.
groups.source_review: Official 2020 WhatsApp hosting explanation and 2025 processor terms checked. Historical hosting claims explicitly dated rather than conflated with all current Cloud API configurations.
groups.notes: Corrected the original implication that business access itself disproves E2EE, and removed blanket automatic Meta advertising use and key-possession claims.

groups.high: Telegram's Privacy Policy distinguishes message content from metadata associated with account and service use. Section 5.2 says Telegram may collect metadata such as IP addresses, devices and Telegram apps used, and username-change history to improve account security and prevent spam, abuse, and Terms of Service violations. If collected under this provision, that metadata may be retained for a maximum of 12 months. An IP address is a network identifier; device and app information describe the software or equipment used. These records can reveal aspects of service use without being the message text itself. Their privacy significance should not be dismissed merely because they are called metadata, nor should the policy be treated as proof of an undisclosed packet-analysis or device-fingerprinting algorithm. Telegram also distinguishes cloud chats from Secret Chats. Cloud-chat messages, photos, videos, and documents are stored on Telegram servers for cross-device access; encryption in transit and storage is not the same as end-to-end encryption. Secret Chats use end-to-end encryption and are not stored as cloud-chat histories. The metadata provision therefore does not justify the claim that all Telegram message contents are inaccessible to Telegram. Section 5.3 additionally describes review of messages reported by recipients and automated analysis of cloud chats to counter spam and phishing. The 12-month maximum concerns the specified security metadata, not a universal retention promise for every category of data. Review the current policy and chat type before assuming that either message encryption or account deletion removes every privacy risk.
groups.mid: Metadata describes how you use a service. It is different from the message text itself. Telegram's Privacy Policy lists some security metadata in Section 5.2. This includes IP addresses, devices and Telegram apps used, and username-change history. An IP address is a network identifier. Device and app details describe your equipment or software. Telegram says these records help protect accounts and prevent spam, abuse, and breaches of its Terms of Service. If collected under Section 5.2, this metadata can be kept for at most 12 months. Such records can still reveal aspects of your use. Calling them metadata does not make them harmless. But the policy does not prove that a particular fingerprinting or packet-analysis system is used. You also need to know your chat type. Cloud chats are not Secret Chats. Telegram stores cloud-chat messages, photos, videos, and documents on its servers. This lets you access them on different devices. Encryption in transit and storage is not the same as end-to-end encryption. Secret Chats use end-to-end encryption. They are not kept as cloud-chat histories. So you should not assume that Telegram cannot access any message content. Section 5.3 describes checking messages that recipients report. It also describes automated analysis of cloud chats to fight spam and phishing. Phishing means trying to trick people into giving away private information. The 12-month maximum applies to the security metadata in Section 5.2. It is not a promise about every type of Telegram data. Check the current policy and the type of chat before making privacy assumptions.
groups.low: A message has words in it. There can also be data about how you use the app. That is called metadata. In Section 5.2 of its Privacy Policy, Telegram says it may collect your IP address, the devices and Telegram apps you use, and your history of username changes. An IP address is a code for a network connection. Device and app details show what phone, computer, or software you use. Telegram says this helps keep accounts safe and stop spam, abuse, and breaches of its Terms of Service. If it collects this data under Section 5.2, it can keep it for no more than 12 months. This data may still tell someone things about your use. Calling it metadata does not make it harmless. But the policy does not tell us that a named secret tracking system is used. Also, not all Telegram chats work the same way. Cloud chats are kept on Telegram's servers. This includes messages, photos, videos, and files, so you can get them on more than one device. Data can be encrypted while it is sent or stored without being end-to-end encrypted. Secret Chats use end-to-end encryption. They are not kept as cloud-chat histories. So do not assume that Telegram cannot access any chat contents. Section 5.3 says it may check messages people report. It also says it may use automated analysis of cloud chats to stop spam and phishing. Phishing means trying to trick people into giving away private details. The 12-month limit is for the security metadata in Section 5.2, not every kind of data. Check which chat type you use and what the policy says.
groups.source_review: Primary policy Sections 3.3, 5.2 and 5.3 checked for chat types, security-metadata categories and maximum retention. Regional policy redirect recorded.
groups.notes: Removed fabricated anonymization guarantees, botnet examples presented as Telegram algorithms, and the false claim that every Telegram chat is E2EE.

groups.high: A sub-processor is another organization engaged to process personal information for a processor. Under the WhatsApp Business Data Processing Terms updated 22 August 2025, these obligations apply where WhatsApp processes the business's customer personal information as its processor. The business is the controller, determining the purposes and means of the processing. The terms require processing according to the contractual instructions, confidentiality for authorized personnel, and appropriate technical and organizational safeguards. WhatsApp may appoint sub-processors through written agreements imposing obligations no less rigorous than its own under these terms, and remains fully liable to the business for their performance. Sub-processors may operate in other countries, including the European Economic Area or the United States; the relevant transfer addenda may therefore matter. Subject to applicable law, changes to sub-processors are notified in advance. A business with a reasonable objection may notify WhatsApp in writing and stop using the Business Services. After termination, the terms require cessation and deletion within the period specified in the Business Terms, subject to legally required storage or an independent right or obligation to use the information. They do not establish an unconditional rule that every message is automatically erased at successful delivery, nor do they identify Redis or a particular memory-queue architecture. Temporary hosting and storage must be understood in the context of the actual service, data category, instructions, and retention terms. A business should establish which providers receive which data, where processing occurs, what deletion rules apply, and how confidentiality and security responsibilities are allocated.
groups.mid: A business may use other providers to help run WhatsApp messaging. A sub-processor is a provider that processes personal information for another processor. The WhatsApp Business Data Processing Terms are dated 22 August 2025. They call the business the controller. It decides why and how customer data is used. WhatsApp is the processor where the Business Terms say it acts in that role. These terms do not cover every possible use of every kind of data. WhatsApp must follow the contract's instructions. Staff allowed to use the data must keep it confidential. Suitable security measures are needed too. WhatsApp may hire a sub-processor. It must use a written agreement. That provider needs duties at least as strict as WhatsApp's own under these terms. WhatsApp remains fully liable to the business for that provider's performance. A provider may be in another country, including the European Economic Area or the United States. The relevant data-transfer addenda can therefore matter. Subject to the law, WhatsApp must give advance notice of sub-processor changes. A business with a reasonable objection can write to WhatsApp and stop using the Business Services. What happens when the contract ends? The terms require processing to stop and deletion within the period in the Business Terms. There are exceptions for storage required by law or an independent right or duty to use the information. This is not a guarantee that every message is erased as soon as it arrives. The terms also do not identify a particular storage tool such as Redis. To assess a setup, ask who receives the data, where it is processed, which deletion rules apply, and who is responsible for confidentiality and security.
groups.low: A business may hire other firms to help send WhatsApp messages. A sub-processor is a firm that handles data for another data processor. Let us look at the WhatsApp Business Data Processing Terms dated 22 August 2025. The business is the controller. That means it decides why and how to use customer data. WhatsApp is the processor when the Business Terms give it that role. These rules apply to that work, not every use of every kind of data. WhatsApp must follow the contract's instructions. Staff allowed to handle the data must keep it confidential. There must also be suitable security steps. If WhatsApp hires a sub-processor, it needs a written agreement. That firm must have duties at least as strict as WhatsApp's duties under these terms. WhatsApp stays fully liable to the business for the firm's work. The firm may be in another country, such as the United States or the European Economic Area. That can make the data-transfer addenda important. An addendum is an extra part of a contract. Subject to the law, WhatsApp must give advance notice when these providers change. A business with a reasonable objection can tell WhatsApp in writing and stop using the Business Services. When the contract ends, processing must stop. Deletion must follow the time stated in the Business Terms. But the law may require some storage, or there may be a separate right or duty to use the data. So do not assume every message is erased as soon as it arrives. The terms do not tell us that a tool such as Redis stores it. Ask which firms get the data, where they handle it, when they delete it, and who must keep it safe and confidential.
groups.source_review: Primary WhatsApp Business Data Processing Terms, last updated 22 August 2025, checked for role scope, written sub-processing contracts, liability, transfers, notices and termination/deletion exceptions.
groups.notes: Removed invented Redis/ephemeral-storage architecture and unconditional purge-on-delivery guarantees. Retained explicit legal role and confidentiality/security distinctions.

groups.high: Amazon's Privacy Notice describes sharing customer information with subsidiaries controlled by Amazon.com, Inc., provided those companies are subject to the notice or follow practices at least as protective as those described in it. A subsidiary is a separate company controlled by another company. This is a condition governing group sharing, not a transfer of ownership over an individual's personal information or permission for unrestricted reuse. Transaction information can include order, payment, delivery, and customer-service details, depending on the activity and applicable notice. Sharing can support functions such as fulfilment, support, and fraud prevention; a claim about a particular use must still be checked against the relevant policy. The clause does not establish that every group company operates an identical database or that sharing eliminates country-specific duties. Requirements for international transfers are a separate question. Controlled subsidiaries must also be distinguished from independent marketplace sellers, advertisers, and outside service providers. This clause is not a blanket assurance about every unrelated recipient. To assess a transaction, identify the recipient's role, the purpose of sharing, the applicable notice, and available account controls or statutory rights. Information supplied during one transaction may reach another qualifying Amazon group company under the protection condition. Similar or stronger protection does not mean no sharing occurs, and it does not authorize every future purpose.
groups.mid: Amazon's Privacy Notice says customer information can go to subsidiaries controlled by Amazon.com, Inc. A subsidiary is a separate company controlled by another company. There is a protection condition. The company must follow the notice. Or it must use practices at least as protective as those in it. That does not mean it owns your personal information. Nor can it use the data for anything it likes. Transaction information is data linked to a purchase or service. It can include details about orders, payments, deliveries, and help with orders. What is shared depends on the activity and notice. Group sharing can support delivery, support, or fraud prevention. But check the policy before assuming a particular use is allowed. The clause does not prove that all the companies use the same database. It does not cancel duties under each country's law. Data may be sent to another country. The rules for that are a separate issue. A controlled subsidiary is not the same as an independent marketplace seller. Advertisers and outside service providers are different too. This clause is not a promise about every unrelated recipient. Ask which company gets your data. What is its role? Why does it need the data? Read the notice that applies. Check the account controls or legal rights available to you. Information from one transaction may go to another Amazon group company covered by this rule. Similar or stronger protection is a condition on sharing. It does not mean no sharing happens, or that every future use is allowed.
groups.low: Your information may go to another company in Amazon's group. Amazon's Privacy Notice calls these subsidiaries controlled by Amazon.com, Inc. A subsidiary is a separate company that another company controls. But there is a condition. It must follow the notice. Or it must use practices at least as protective as those in it. That does not mean it owns your data. It cannot just use the data for anything it likes. Transaction data is data linked to a purchase or service. It may include details about orders, payments, deliveries, or help with orders. What is shared depends on the activity and notice. Group sharing can help with delivery, support, or fraud prevention. Check the policy before assuming a use is allowed. The clause does not prove that all the companies have the same database. They still have to meet duties under each country's law. Data may be sent to another country. The rules for that are a separate question. A company Amazon controls is not the same as an independent seller. An advertiser or outside service provider is different too. So this clause is not a promise about every firm that gets data. Ask which company gets your data. What is its role? Why does it need the data? Read the notice that applies. Check the account choices or legal rights you can use. Data from one transaction may go to another Amazon group company covered by this rule. Similar or stronger protection is a condition on sharing. It does not mean there is no sharing or allow every future use.
groups.source_review: Official Amazon notice URL returned HTTP 503 during this pass. Core controlled-subsidiary/protection condition is retained from supplied topic/reference; current edition and particular purposes require further primary-page verification.
groups.notes: Removed false legal ownership claim and invented mandatory group data architecture/contracts. Source-access limitation is explicit; this is not marked comprehensively verified.
